local_facts.claim: Phoenix’s 2025 Water Quality Report lists total hardness at 172–302 ppm, or 10–17.6 grains per gallon, and says hard water can cause scaling in pipes, water heaters, and plumbing fixtures.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Mineral scale is a useful condition to inspect in older copper and at fixtures when pressure or water-loss symptoms appear. It is not proof of a pinhole leak, so the technician still isolates and tests the affected system before recommending a repair.
local_facts.title: Phoenix water carries enough minerals to leave plumbing scale

local_facts.claim: Phoenix Water Services says its Sewer Fee Review may adjust a sewer fee when higher-than-usual water use is caused by broken plumbing or outdoor irrigation equipment. For the 2026 review, requests received more than 60 days after the July bill date are not eligible, and prior years cannot be adjusted.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A sudden City Services bill is often the first practical sign of a hidden leak. Keeping bills and repair records gives a homeowner the documentation needed to check current eligibility, while prompt detection prevents additional loss.
local_facts.title: A bill spike has a time-sensitive city review path

local_facts.claim: The Arizona Geological Survey says groundwater withdrawal can drive land subsidence and earth-fissure formation, and lists Maricopa County among counties that host earth fissures. It notes that fissures can damage utility lines, roads, and canals.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Ground movement is a reason to carefully evaluate a buried water-line route when testing points outside the house. It does not diagnose a fissure or establish the cause of a specific leak; the pipe still needs evidence-based detection at the property.
local_facts.title: Buried lines in Maricopa County may face changing ground conditions

pricing.table_head: Phoenix leak work, job by job

anchors.label: City position on customer side leaks
anchors.detail: The code makes each customer responsible for all leaks downstream of the point of service delivery, and for full payment of charges for any water lost to those leaks. There is no water leak credit program to apply for.

anchors.label: Water in the high use season
anchors.detail: The June through September rate for an inside city account, against $4.93 in the low season, on top of a $4.64 monthly service charge on a five eighths inch meter. One hundred cubic feet is 748 gallons.
anchors.source_name: City of Phoenix water rates effective March 2025

anchors.label: Sewer fee review window
anchors.detail: Sewer charges are recalculated each July from average January through March water use. A review requested more than 60 days after that July bill date is ineligible, with no exceptions stated.
anchors.source_name: City of Phoenix sewer fee review

anchors.label: Minimum residential permit fee
anchors.detail: The schedule adopted in December 2025 sets a $195 minimum permit fee for single lot residential construction, includes the first re-inspection, and charges $195 for each re-inspection after that.
anchors.source_name: City of Phoenix development fee schedule
